blocks.heading: Markets connect buyers and sellers
blocks.text:
A market is an arrangement bringing buyers and sellers into contact to exchange a product or resource. Buyers seek something they want and sellers offer it on terms they are willing to consider. Contact allows information about the product, quantity and payment to pass between them. The arrangement can exist without a sale being completed in every conversation: potential buyers may compare offers or decide not to buy. What matters is the connection through which exchange can be arranged.

A market is therefore broader than a building or a row of stalls. A vegetable stall is one familiar example, but a repair service booked remotely can also participate in a market. Markets can concern goods, services or resources such as labour. In each case identify what is being exchanged and who occupies each side. A person looking for paid work offers labour services, while an employer seeks those services. Saying that someone is a buyer in one transaction does not mean they cannot be a seller in another. The same household may buy groceries and supply labour.

blocks.heading: Physical and digital contact
blocks.text:
Physical and digital describe ways of bringing buyers and sellers together. In a physical arrangement, customers can visit a location and discuss a product in person. In a digital arrangement, electronic communication can let customers view offers and place orders at a distance. These channels can overlap. An invented tailor might take measurements at a shop, show available fabrics through an online catalogue and confirm collection electronically. That combination does not create three separate products or require three separate sellers. It shows different stages of one trading arrangement.

To classify a case, inspect how contact and ordering occur rather than the payment method alone. A customer using a bank card at a physical stall has not thereby turned the stall into a digital marketplace. Conversely, an online order collected and paid for in cash still used digital contact to arrange the sale. Payment, communication and delivery are related parts of a transaction, but they answer different questions. A successful channel must make exchange workable for the relevant people: attractive pictures are insufficient if customers cannot obtain accurate information or receive the goods.

blocks.heading: A choice of access
blocks.text: An invented seller of handmade bags could reach local passers-by at a stall and distant customers through electronic orders. Direct inspection may matter when customers want to check stitching. Distance ordering may matter when travelling to the stall is difficult. Neither channel is automatically cheaper or better: travel, operating hours, access, delivery and confidence affect the comparison. This links to exchange in topic 2.3 and introduces the buyer and seller decisions analysed in market forces in topic 3.2. First establish the market arrangement; then explain how the relevant information and constraints influence exchange. A market description should name the product and the people connected. A building with no arrangement for buyer-seller exchange is not established as a market merely because people gather there.
